live: Solar wind at L1, measured by SOLAR1: Bz -9.1 nanotesla (strongly southward, which couples energy into the magnetosphere); total field 9.9 nT; speed 486 kilometres per second; density 21.0 protons per cubic centimetre. Measured [E], timestamped 18:03 UTC, 7 min old.

That wind was measured at L1, about 1.5 million kilometres sunward, and takes roughly an hour to arrive. NOAA propagates it to the bow shock nose [D · NOAA]: what is reaching Earth right now was observed at 17:20 UTC, with Bz -8.0 nT and speed 490 km/s. There are about 40 minutes of already-measured wind still in flight — that is the warning currently in hand.

GOES-19 measures 96 nT at geostationary orbit, 6.6 Earth radii out [E], 18:05 UTC. That is 12 nT below the dipole value for that distance; the difference is the ring current and magnetopause currents subtracting from Earth's own field. The modelled boundary is outside 6.6 Rₑ, so the spacecraft should be inside the magnetosphere, which is what this field says.

Energetic particles at geostationary orbit, measured by GOES [E], 18:00 UTC: protons above 10 MeV at 0.30 pfu, radiation storm level S0 (None). Electrons above 2 MeV at 1400 pfu, above NOAA’s alert level for satellite charging.
Planetary K index 5.33 — geomagnetic conditions are minor storm. Measured [E], 18:01 UTC.

Ring current index Dst -64 nanotesla — moderate storm. This is how much a torus of trapped ions drifting around Earth is subtracting from the surface field; it is the single number that best tracks the size of a storm. Modelled [D] by NOAA's Geospace run from the L1 solar wind — not Kyoto's measured index, which has no route into a browser — for 18:09 UTC. The model runs 25 minutes ahead of that; the value quoted is the newest one whose time has arrived, not the newest one in the file.
Solar X-ray background is class M1.2 (1.2e-5 watts per square metre, 0.1–0.8 nanometre band, GOES). Measured [E], 18:04 UTC.
NOAA scales today: radio blackouts R1 (Minor), solar radiation S0 (None), geomagnetic storms G2 (Moderate). NOAA's own product, modeled [D].

Modeled [D] magnetopause standoff: 8.4 Earth radii on the sunward side, with flaring parameter 0.60, computed from the propagated solar wind above (dynamic pressure 4.20 nanopascals) using Shue et al. 1998, doi:10.1029/98JA01103. That is a compressed magnetosphere — the shield is being pushed in. The bow shock stands off at 10.9 Earth radii (Farris & Russell 1994).
Most recent NOAA notice, 12:00 UTC: K-index of 5. 1 notices in the last three days.

2 cones are drawn expanding from the Sun [D], warm where Earth lies inside the cone and cool where it does not. The apex direction, half-angle and speed are DONKI's analysis of coronagraph imagery; the radial propagation is ours.

Scene: the Sun at centre, with all eight planets at their true positions for 18:10 UTC, computed locally with astronomy-engine [D]. The Sun is currently overhead at 5.9°N, 93.0°W, and Earth's day/night terminator in the scene is drawn from that point [D]. The Moon is shown at its true direction from Earth.

Earth's surface is measured imagery [E]: NASA's Blue Marble Next Generation composite, acquired through 2004, with NASA's Black Marble 2016 night lights drawn as emission on the night side. Nothing about it is live — it is a dated composite, and it says so here rather than pretending to be today's clouds.
Aurora: the OVATION forecast is unavailable, so no oval is drawn.

The magnetic shield is drawn: 80 field lines traced through IGRF-14 (IAGA, epoch 2025.0, secular variation to now) [D], blue where they close between hemispheres and violet where they stay open toward the solar wind. The teal boundary is the Shue et al. 1998 magnetopause and the orange one the Farris & Russell 1994 bow shock, both re-shaped by the live solar wind above. Added to it is Tsyganenko 1989 (T89c), external field, Kp-driven — no IMF dependence [D], band 6 of 7, Kp 5−, 5, 5+, at a dipole tilt of 12.7°. That is what compresses the dayside, stretches the nightside into lobes and inflates the inner region: the shape is the field's, integrated, not a surface drawn around a dipole. This is the fallback — the solar wind was incomplete, so T96 could not run. T89 bins Kp into seven fits, so the field steps between them rather than gliding, and it carries no IMF term at all: a southward Bz opens the real dayside and changes nothing here. 4 lines run past where they are drawn, and are cut rather than ended: T89 is fitted inside 70 Rₑ and has no magnetopause, so the trace stops at the edge of what the model describes — down the tail, and 20 Rₑ sunward. The boundary surfaces stop at 100° from the sunward axis, inside the range Shue et al. fitted; the real magnetotail continues far beyond.

Globe scale — distances log-compressed, bodies enlarged. Camera: Deck — Behind Earth looking back down the Sun–Earth line: both bodies in frame, with the wind and the field lines running between them. Motion is enabled.

The streaming particles are ambient [M] — far sparser and brighter than the real wind, which is invisible. What is real is their behaviour: they move at a rate set by the measured 486 km/s, their number follows the measured density, and they part around the same modelled magnetopause the HUD reports. When the boundary is pushed in, the flow closes in with it.
The field lines are shivering. That is ambient [M] — a legend for the elevated Kp above, not a motion the real field makes.

Colour and the starfield are ambient [M] — parameter-driven artwork, not measurements. There is no invented glow around the Sun: the region a painted corona would have occupied is the region the LASCO coronagraphs actually photograph, and that imagery is shown there instead when it is switched on.
